name: BDDE crosslinked HA

card.summary: Hyaluronic acid gel stabilised with the crosslinker BDDE, the basis of most dermal fillers used to add volume to lips, cheeks, jawline and chin.
card.aka: BDDE, 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether crosslinked hyaluronic acid
card.note: Filler complications include rare vascular occlusion; procedures belong with qualified clinicians.

quick.overview:
Natural hyaluronic acid (HA) breaks down within a short time in tissue. Manufacturers link HA chains with a crosslinker, most commonly BDDE, so the gel lasts months and holds its shape. This crosslinked gel is what is injected as a dermal filler to restore or add volume.

In appearance terms, BDDE-crosslinked HA is behind fuller lips, defined cheeks, a sharper jawline and chin projection. A review of its metabolism reports that, after reaction, only trace unreacted BDDE (under 2 parts per million) remains and that the gel breaks down to substances already found in skin; trials registered for lips, jawline and midface fillers continue to study its performance.
quick.how: The gel is injected by a trained clinician into specific facial layers, and effects typically last several months to about a year depending on product and area, after which treatment may be repeated. Fillers are usually sold by brand and gel type, with firmer gels used for structure (jaw, chin) and softer ones for lips and fine lines. Practitioners can dissolve HA fillers with the enzyme hyaluronidase.
quick.risks: Common effects are bruising, redness, pain and itching; less often infection, lumps or allergic reactions; rarely vascular occlusion leading to skin necrosis or blindness. A reference source notes a study linking BDDE to allergic reactions in some patients, while a dermatologic review concludes the safety record over 15 years is favourable. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.

lead: BDDE (1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether) is a chemical crosslinker used to join chains of hyaluronic acid into a durable gel. Most HA dermal fillers are crosslinked this way to slow breakdown and prolong results [1][5]. Wikipedia notes that the crosslinking method affects stability, degradation and retention time [5].

For appearance, the crosslinked gel is injected to enhance lips, cheeks and jawline and to smooth folds [5]. Registered trials include a lip filler investigation, a jawline contour study and a midface volume study, reflecting these uses [6][7][8].

A 2013 review of BDDE-crosslinked HA metabolism found the reacted gel contains less than 2 ppm free BDDE and degrades into harmless or skin-native byproducts, concluding that over 15 years of data support its safety profile [1]. Other work notes concern: Wikipedia cites a 2015 study reporting BDDE-linked allergic reactions in 34.3% of 452 patients and a 2024 review raising long-term safety questions [5]. Industry reviews discuss the specifications of an ideal crosslinker [2].

chain: Gel persists in tissue for months
Injected volume enhances lips, cheeks, jaw
angle.text: The crosslinking gives HA a long enough residence time and firmness to be placed as filler. Clinicians inject it to add volume or definition to lips, cheeks, jawline and chin.

infobox: Fillers are medical devices (FDA, CE mark)

paras: Unmodified HA degrades quickly in the body, so manufacturers crosslink it. BDDE forms ether bonds between HA chains that resist hydrolysis, supporting long-term integrity [4][5]. An industry review notes that few papers discuss crosslinkers themselves despite wide filler use and outlines properties of an ideal one [2].

HA fillers are used cosmetically for wrinkles and folds, volume loss, and enhancement of lips, cheeks and jawline, with firmer fillers placed deeper [5]. Registered trials examine lip augmentation, jawline contour deficit, midface volume deficit and nasolabial folds [6][7][8][9].

The 2013 review reported that residual BDDE is below 2 ppm and degradation products are benign [1]. A rat study examined perineural application of BDDE-crosslinked HA because adverse events with crosslinked HA have been documented [3]. Common filler effects include bruising, redness, pain and itching; rare outcomes are infection, allergic reaction, vascular embolisation causing blindness, and delayed necrosis [5].
In the US fillers are medical devices requiring a clinician; only a handful are approved. In the UK and EU many fillers carry a CE mark, which certifies production standards rather than efficacy [5].
BDDE-HA is used as a matrix in experimental composites for regenerative soft-tissue reconstruction [10] and in microspheres for embolisation research [11].

Registered post-market investigations in Europe include a jawline contour trial (n=114) and a midface volume trial (n=111), both completed [7][8], a lip trial (n=100) ongoing [6], and a Restylane nasolabial fold study (n=10) [9]. The metabolism review summarises longer-term clinical and biocompatibility data [1].

timeline.event: Hyaluronic acid first isolated from bovine vitreous by Meyer and Palmer.[4]
Review of BDDE-crosslinked HA metabolism published.[1]
